leads.name: Kyle Auction Oak
leads.species: Live Oak (Quercus virginiana or Quercus fusiformis, not yet settled)
leads.reason: The town of Kyle was sold off under this oak in 1880: the railroad auctioned the business and most residential lots in its shade and ran free trains from Austin to draw buyers. The county historical commission braced it after it began to split. Downtown Kyle at 204 S. Sledge Street, about 34 km from central Austin, slightly past the 30 km line; decide container before writing. RESOLVED 2026-09-27, verify pass: existence/species/history confirmed by 4 independent sources beyond the finding aid (official Texas Historical Marker #10289 text, Kyle Chamber of Commerce, a 2014 Hays Free Press news story naming the Hays County Historical Commission ecology chairman who had it cross-braced and cabled after a canopy split, and a dated 2019 visitor account with on-site photos and GPS). Species: Live Oak, exact variety not settled by any source. ALIVE: confirmed in 2014 (active professional preservation, named source) and again by a personal visit in 2019; nothing found suggests removal since, and the Chamber still lists it today, but no observation from the last few years exists, so any use should flag that gap. ACCESS: the tree stands on private residential land at 204 S. Sledge Street (a 2019 visitor: "Being on personal property, I did not feel comfortable clawing around"), but the historical marker and the tree itself are in front of the house, viewable and photographable from the public street/sidewalk; a view-only entry (pin at the viewing place, access line stating plainly it stands on private land and is seen from the street) would be honest if this ever ships. CONTAINER, the open question: NOT Austin. No public transport connects Kyle to Austin at all today, so the ~30-minutes-by-public-transport day-trip test cannot be honestly claimed regardless of the 34km driving distance: Capital MetroRail's lines run nowhere near Kyle (the Green Line under construction serves NE Austin/Colony Park, unrelated direction); the Lone Star Rail District commuter-rail plan for the Austin-Kyle-San Marcos-San Antonio corridor died in 2016 when Union Pacific withdrew, and a 2024 revival push has produced no service; CARTS, the regional rural transit agency, explicitly does not serve Kyle as an urbanized-area stop (only a once-a-week Country Bus route touches Kyle from Dripping Springs/Wimberley). NOT its own place either, on balance: this is a well-loved, actively-preserved local landmark with a genuine town-founding story and an official state historical marker, but nothing found suggests people travel to Kyle specifically for this one tree the way they would for an Angel Oak or a Bartram's Ginkgo, so it likely does not clear the single-famous-tree exception (2026-08-31) on its own. Stays a lead: worth a look again if Kyle ever accumulates enough separately-verified trees to reach its own four-tree floor, or if a future "day trips" collection wants a well-documented outlier.
sources: https://texashistoricalmarkers.weebly.com/kyle-auction-oak.html (quotes official Texas Historical Marker No. 10289 text in full)
https://www.kylechamber.org/historical-sites (Kyle Area Chamber of Commerce, current official listing)
https://www.carolynhestand.com/blog/kyle-auction-oak (dated visitor account, 2019-10-20, with photo and on-site GPS)

blocked.name: Quercus sinuata var. breviloba, Texas Big Tree Registry TreeID 970
sources: Texas Big Tree Registry, Texas A&M Forest Service (texasforestinfo.tamu.edu/BigTreeRegistry). Non-commercial licence: usable as a lead and verification source, never imported. See OPEN_DATA_SURVEY.md.
blocked.why_blocked: PRIVATE LAND. The Texas Big Tree Registry's PublicOrPrivate flag is 0 on this tree, and the flag is not the undocumented mystery an earlier pass took it for: across all 660 swept trees, flag 1 belongs to Big Bend and Guadalupe Mountains National Parks, Sam Houston National Forest, state natural areas and TxDOT districts, while flag 0 belongs to Big Tree Ranch, X-Arrow Ranch, Little Sandy Hunting & Fishing Club and similar. It means what it says. The registry also sets Display 0 on almost all of them, so it withholds these locations from its own public map, and hard rule 10 is absolute about not undoing that: the coordinates only reached us because the backend returns what the front end hides. Never ship unless a source shows the site is genuinely open to visitors.

notes.note: Swept from the corrected Texas Big Tree Registry pull (scripts/texas_big_trees.py). Circumference is INCHES: an earlier Houston pass read it as centimetres and concluded the state was thin. Coordinates decide which city a tree belongs to, never CountyName.

PublicOrPrivate decoded from the data itself: flag 1 is national parks, national forests, state natural areas and TxDOT; flag 0 is ranches and hunting clubs. Flag 0 trees moved to blocked under hard rule 10, since the registry also hides them from its own public map and their coordinates only reached us because the backend returns what the front end withholds. OrganizationName names the owner and is the field a verify pass should lead with.
